narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 66.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and wants students likely to succeed, this probability led to your application being rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your academic performance in law school, your undergraduate grades, and your first-year law school performance. Your third-year law school ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) compared to an average of about 5.8 among accepted students signaled that your later-year performance was significantly below the level the model associates with passing the bar. Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction, modestly pulling the prediction toward success, yet its positive effect was not enough to offset the other signals. Your first-year law school ranking also contributed noticeably toward failure, as your bottom-decile placement (1 versus an average of 6 among accepted students) reinforced the pattern of academic struggle.

Taken together, these academic indicators outweighed other details such as your LSAT score of 26.5 (well below the accepted average of 37), your low family income, and your plan to attend full-time.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses, consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score, and explore schools or programs with different admissions thresholds. You may also want to speak with an admissions counselor about what specific improvements would make your profile competitive in a future cycle. (248 words)
